[Source 1 — www.dailymail.com] (URL: https://www.dailymail.com/news/article-16225427/aldi-self-checkout-closures-shelves-staff-burnout.html?ns_mchannel=rss&ns_campaign=1490&ito=1490):
Stated Claim / Post Context:
I'm an Aldi manager and Aussies complain and abuse me about empty shelves and unmanned checkouts - but they have no idea about the cost cutting happening behind the scenes

An Aldi manager has exposed why many Aussies are growing frustrated with the supermarket chain.

Actual Article Body:
By BURNEY WONG - NEWS REPORTER

Published:  10:41 AEDT, 23 October 2026   |  Updated:  10:56 AEDT, 23 October 2026

An Aldi manager has lifted the lid on what they claim is happening behind the scenes at the German supermarket giant, revealing why frustrated shoppers are facing long checkout queues, empty shelves and disappearing products.

Speaking out on social media, the employee claimed sweeping cost-cutting measures and staff shortages had left workers overwhelmed, with some stores struggling to keep shelves stocked while employees rush between checkouts and other duties.

The manager said conditions had deteriorated significantly over the past two years, leaving even long-serving staff questioning their future with the company.

'Over the past year or two, stores have been put through a lot of changes coming from higher up. None of us in stores, whether staff or management, are happy about it. Most of us are burnt out and hating our jobs.'

One of the biggest frustrations for shoppers is the closure of self-service checkouts, sometimes leaving customers waiting in a lengthy queue for a single staffed register.

But according to the manager, employees are just as frustrated, claiming stores simply aren't allocated enough staff hours to keep the machines operating throughout the day.

'We think its stupid too... Self checkouts are self checkouts for a reason. Whats the point in having them if they can't even be used half the time.

'Sadly we are not given enough hours in store to man the self checkout from open to close.

An Aldi manager has urged customers not to take out their anger on supermarket workers. Stock image of an Aldi worker. Not the worker making the complaints

'The self checkout person has to close it off when its less busy to go do other work or we don't complete our jobs for the day and the store suffers.

'Even the self checkout person has a bunch of work they need to get done while also opening up the self checkouts when required. We would love to keep it open all day but we just can't with the amount of hours we are given. I won't even get started on the new self checkout scale problems.'

And it's not just the checkouts causing headaches.

The manager claimed Aldi was quietly reducing the range of products available to customers, with popular items disappearing from shelves as the company prioritised stocking larger quantities of fewer products.

'Aldi is removing a lot of products from the shelves with the idea of having even less total products and just increasing the amount of facings/total stock of the other "core" items.

'This is all in the name of making stock easier to fill up as there is less variety of items which is yet again, another justification they have to cut more hours.'

The employee also offered an explanation for another familiar frustration among shoppers: arriving at Aldi to discover empty spaces on the shelves.

While some products were genuinely unavailable, the manager claimed others were sitting in storerooms because there weren't enough workers to put them out.

A manager of over five years urged customers to lodge complaints over a raft of changes they claimed have left staff, management and customers increasingly frustrated

'Some of these are due to stock being unavailable despite it being ordered, but half the time it's literally just due to a lack of hours,' they wrote.

'Quite often now, there's only two to four staff on at certain times of day and it's not uncommon for all of them to be on the registers and self-checkout.

'That leaves nobody on the shop floor to fill gaps on the shelves even though we may have stock out in the back, nobody to help customers and limited time for managers to do their rushed stock take.'

The manager claimed shoppers had also begun noticing a decline in the quality of some products, with staff regularly fielding complaints about once-popular items that had changed.

'Most of our staff has gotten feedback from a customer here and there about a product they loved, which has changed and become terrible,' they wrote.

'We are powerless in this as not even the store manager has any say at all in this.'

The employee claimed their own store had been allocated more than 25 per cent fewer staff hours than it had just 18 months earlier, despite workers still being expected to complete their daily duties.

'To put it simply, most staff and managers in stores are growing increasingly unhappy with the company and burning out.

Aussies have lashed out at changes to Aldi stores after an Aldi manager said self-checkout closures and staffing pressures were among several issues frustrating customers and burning out workers

The managerurged customers not to lash out at staff.

'A lot of our customers are growing increasingly unhappy. We deal with upset, frustrated and sometimes angry and abusive customers regularly.

'If anything bothers you in store, please don't take it out on the staff, we're miserable enough as it is and we have no say in any business changes, not even the store manager.

'We would love to present a nice tidy store with full shelves and helpful staff but that is becoming less and less possible with the decrease in hours and extreme cutting of costs.'

The worker instead urged frustrated customers to lodge their complaints directly with the German supermarket chain through its website.

'Its a s**t show in stores right now and this isn't even taking into account many behind the scenes changes in our work.'

The explosive claims struck a nerve with shoppers, with several Australians sharing similar experiences at their local Aldi stores.

'There have been times where I have stopped off at Aldi on the way home, walked in, saw the self-serve checkouts closed with only one staff checkout open with a huge line and walked out immediately,' one wrote.

'The whole self-checkout implementation has been a disaster for customers and I just hate going to Aldi now,' another wrote.

Others said their biggest frustration wasn't the queues or staff shortages, but what they perceived as a decline in Aldi's quality of food.

'To be honest the biggest disappointment is not the staff, checkouts, less products - but the sheer drop in quality, first meat, then vegetables, then dairy, electronics break after few weeks or a couple of months and the saving comparing to Coles and Co is absolutely minimal these days,' one Aussie said.

An Aldi spokesman told Daily Mail the supermarket regularly reviewed how its stores operated to ensure they had the right staff and resources to serve customers effectively.

He defended the company's streamlined operating model, saying efficiency had always been central to Aldi's ability to offer lower prices.

'Like any retailer, the way we operate continues to evolve, but we have always run a lean store operation, with everything from product design, packaging and even bar code placement on products curated to make our stores more efficient,' he said.

'Decisions around team structures and checkout options consider the needs of individual stores, while maintaining the simple and efficient operating model that allows us to keep prices low.

'The wellbeing of our people is of the utmost important to us, and we take feedback from our teams seriously.'

Aussie Borlase on winning side as Atlanta Dream leads WNBA Finals

Australian basketballer Izzy Borlase is one step closer to a WNBA title as her Atlanta Dream side beats Golden State Valkyries to lead 2-1 in the best-of-seven WNBA Finals.

Actual Article Body:
Emergency

Backstory

Newsletters

中文新闻

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

TOK PISIN

Sport

Topic:Basketball

Izzy Borlase scored 12 points in 26 minutes on-court, as her Atlanta Dream side took a 2-1 lead in the WNBA Finals. (Getty Images: Colin Hubbard)

Australia's Izzy Borlase made a solid contribution as her Atlanta Dream team hit the front in the WNBA Finals.

Borlase scored 12 points with five rebounds, while star Angel Reese had 21 points and 12 rebounds, as the Dream beat Golden State Valkyries 97-71 to lead the series 2-1.

Game 4 of the best-of-seven WNBA Finals will be played in Atlanta on Sunday (AEDT).

Angel Reese recorded 21 points and 12 rebounds to help the Atlanta Dream secure a 97-71 home victory over the Golden State Valkyries, giving the Dream a 2-1 lead in the WNBA Finals after Game 3.

Rhyne Howard added 16 points, and Naz Hillmon had 15 for the Dream, who also host Game 4 on Sunday (AEDT).

Australian guard Izzy Borlase played a solid role for the Dream on Wednesday night, local time. She played 26 minutes, finishing with 12 points, including one three-pointer, plus five rebounds, two assists and a block.

Another Australian Opals star, Miela Sowah, sat on the bench for the Valkyries and will remain there throughout the finals due to her restricted status as a development player.

The Dream highlighted one of Borlase's drives to the basket on its social media.

It was the second straight strong game for Reese, who had 30 points and 16 rebounds in Game 2, which the Dream also won for its first-ever victory in the Finals. She now has a double-double in each game of the Finals.

"It feels good when you're in the finals. It's a long season, and you play against everybody and go through and push through, but when you can do it at the highest level, this is what you live for, this is what the off-season is for," Reese said.

"I put the work in for this moment, and I'm just happy I could lead the team to a win. We're feeling good going into Saturday."

With the game tied at 49 in the third quarter, Atlanta scored eight straight, including four by Reese. Golden State got within 59-55 on Tiffany Hayes's lay-up, but could get no closer as Atlanta closed the quarter, scoring 12 of the final 14 points.

With Atlanta up 17 in the fourth quarter, Jordin Canada overthrew Reese on the break, but she saved the ball by throwing it over her head underneath the basket to Howard, who got fouled.

Email us abcsport5050@your.abc.net.au

Golden State could never recover. Gabby Williams scored 15 points, and Hayes added 14 for the Valkyries.

"Protect home court," Howard said of the team's focus. "Giving our fans a show. We fought for this arena so we had to protect it. It's big. We went and stole one, but we can't let them come in and do the same thing."

The game was moved from the Dream's home Gateway Center Arena to the NBA's Atlanta Hawks home arena. Wednesday night's game was sold out, with more than 17,000 fans attending, as is Game 4 on Saturday at the same venue.

The game got off to a slow start as Atlanta led 9-1 after the first five minutes. Golden State missed its first eight shots before Aminata Gueye scored the first basket with 4:39 left.

They got within 13-10 before Naz Hillmon hit consecutive 3-pointers and then Reese hit one. The Dream led 23-15 after the opening quarter.

Atlanta built its lead to 37-26 midway through the period. Golden State was able to hang around and only trailed 46-40 at the break as the teams combined to shoot 15-for-31 (48 per cent) from behind the arc.

That was more completed 3-pointers in the first 20 minutes than in either Game 1 or Game 2.

Game 1 and 2 had huge ratings, with the opener on NBC averaging 2.1 million, the most ever for a first game of the Finals. Game 2, which was broadcast on USA Network, averaged 1.33 million viewers.
